markup: Why were the Directives included in the Constitution?
answermarkup:
i. After independence, India faced the following challenges:
a. Establishing order
b. Carrying out smooth administration
c. Eradication of social issues like poverty, backwardness and illiteracy
d. The task of building a nation
e. Achieving welfare of people
Basically, the nation had to be transformed into a developed and progressive one.
ii. To achieve all this, creating and implementing new policies was imperative.
iii. These policies had to be such that they urgently addressed certain aspects of public welfare. Hence, these aspects needed priority.
iv. The subjects to which the Union and State Governments should give priority in their public welfare policies were specified through the Directive Principles of State policy.
Due to the above reasons, the Directives were included in the Constitution.

markup: What warning did Shivaji Maharaj issue to his soldiers to avoid any loss to the ryot?
answermarkup:
i. Shivaji Maharaj cared about his ryot and took every measure to prevent any loss to them. He issued strict warnings to his soldiers for their safety.
ii. Generally, in case of a war, during the sowing-growing-reaping period of crops, the movements of army interfered with the work of farmers, causing a huge loss to the farmers.
iii. Moreover, soldiers would cut off and take away the standing crops or would destroy them and rob the houses of the farmers. Shivaji Maharaj prohibited such actions ensuring that his soldiers caused no harm to his ryot.
iv. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj also wrote a letter in 1674 CE to his military officers regarding this. This shows how minutely he thought about the welfare of the ryot under his Swaraj.

markup: Describe the role of Chhatrapati Rajaram Maharaj in continuing the Maratha War of Independence.
answermarkup:

2.	He escaped from Raigad and reached Jinji fort safely to continue the war.
3.	He appointed capable generals like Santaji Ghorpade and Dhanaji Jadhav.
4.	Under his leadership, Marathas attacked Mughal territories using guerrilla tactics.
5.	His efforts kept the struggle for Swaraj alive until his death in 1700 CE.

markup: How will human dignity be established in a society?
answermarkup:
i) Human dignity means equal respect to each individual as a human being irrespective of their caste, creed, race, sex, language, etc.
ii) Just as we expect others to treat us with dignity and respect, we should also treat others with the same dignity and respect.
iii) Thus, human dignity will be established in a society only when every individual respects another and honours their freedom and rights. This ultimately leads to growth of fraternity.

markup: What is meant by Right to Constitutional Remedies?
answermarkup:
i. The Indian citizens' right to get judicial remedies, in case of encroachment upon their fundamental rights, is called as the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
ii. When an encroachment upon our rights which are guaranteed by the Constitution, prevents us from exercising our rights, it is called as an infringement of our rights.
iii. Constitution itself has provided for legal remedies in such cases and it is the duty of the courts to protect the rights of the people.
iv. For this, the court considers our complaint, investigates it and gives an appropriate verdict.

markup: Write short notes on : The impact of Sant Basaveshwar's work on society.
answermarkup:
The impact of Sant Basaveshwar's work on society is stated as follows:
i) Sant Basaveshwar was a proponent of the Bhakti movement and spread the lingayat stream of thought in Karnataka.
ii) He believed in 'Kayakave Kailas' which means 'Work is Kailas' (Work is worship).
iii) He was against the caste system and rather stressed the dignity of labour. Men and women of all caste and creed participated in his movement. He conducted the religious discussions in the hall 'Anubhava Mantapa'.
iv) Through the medium of 'Vachana' literature, he conveyed his teachings in Kannada- the language of the people. His followers composed their work in Marathi as well.
Hence, we can say that, his work had a great impact on the society as a whole.

markup: After the death of Peshwa Madhavrao, which Maratha Sardars set right the disarray of the Maratha State?
answermarkup:
i. After the death of Peshwa Madhavrao, Mahadji Shinde restored the Maratha supremacy in the North.
ii. Nana Phadnavis managed the affairs of the South. In this, he received the help from the Patwardhans, Haripant Phadke, the Rastes and other Sardars and was able to establish Maratha supremacy in the South.
iii. The Holkars of Indore, Bhosales of Nagpur, Shindes of Gwalior, and Gaikwads of Vadodara brought glory to the Maratha power based on their valour, leadership qualities, and capability.

markup: Explain the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
answermarkup:
i) It gives citizens the right to approach the courts if their fundamental rights are violated.
ii) The Supreme Court and High Courts can issue writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari for justice.
iii) It is called the heart and soul of the Constitution because it protects all other rights.
iv) This right ensures that no person or government authority can deny citizens their fundamental rights.

markup: Which actions of Shivaji Maharaj show his revolutionary aspects in the field of religion?
answermarkup:
i. Shivaji Maharaj followed a tolerant religious policy. He equally respected the people of other religions as he respected the people of his own religion.
ii. In spite of an opposition to a reconversion at that time, Shivaji Maharaj brought back the act of swadharma i.e the persons who had converted their original religion to another religion.
iii. At times of religious opposition to crossing the seas, he built sea forts like Singhudurg and created a navy. This was a stratergy of countering foreign invasions through the sea.
iv. Through his coronation, he officially became the ruler of Swaraj, but later, had a second coronation from a different religious perspective.
The above actions of Shivaji Maharaj show his revolutionary aspects in the field of religion.

markup: What are Cultural and Educational Rights?
answermarkup:
i) Every community in India has the right to preserve and promote its language, script, and culture.
ii) People can establish educational institutions for the development of their language and culture.
iii) The government must protect the rights of minorities to run their own educational institutions.
iv) These rights help maintain India’s unity in diversity and protect cultural uniqueness.

markup: What do you understand by 'fundamental rights'?
answermarkup:
i. The Indian Constitution aims to create an atmosphere conducive to the development of the self as well as the entire society for which it guarantees equal rights to all citizens. These rights are fundamental rights.
ii. As they are included in the Constitution, they have the status of a law. Hence, it is equally imperative for everybody to abide by these rights.
iii. These rights make sure that all individuals get protection from injustice, exploitation, discrimination and deprivation.
iv. These rights also ensure that all individuals are able to develop their skills and qualities without any discrimination against any citizen on the grounds of religion, caste, race, sex, descent or place of birth or residence, etc.

markup: How do we know that the religious policy of Shivaji Maharaj was that of tolerance?
answermarkup:
The following instances show that the religious policy of Shivaji Maharaj was that of tolerance:
i. In spite of Shivaji Maharaj's enemies being Islamic powers, he considered the Muslims in the Swaraj as his own subjects and trusted them deeply.
The following are a testimony to the same:
a. Siddi Ibrahim was a trusted servant in his army.
b. Siddi Hilal was a Sardar in his army.
c. Daulatkhan was an important officer in the navy of Swaraj.
ii. He even continued the facilities given to the Muslim places of worship that belonged to the captured enemy territories.
iii. The written work by historian Khafikhan on the tolerant religious policy of Shivaji Maharaj states that: "Shivaji Maharaj had framed strict rules for his soldiers that during the campaigns, they should not harm a mosque. In case, if they came in possession of a copy, of the Holy Quran, they should hand over the same, with reverence, to a Muslim."

markup: What are Directive Principles of State Policy? Explain their importance.
answermarkup:
i) Directive Principles are guidelines given to the State for achieving the goals stated in the Preamble.
ii) They direct the government to frame policies for public welfare and national development.
iii) These principles help to establish economic and social justice in the country.
iv) They aim to create a welfare state where every citizen enjoys equality, dignity, and opportunities for progress.

markup: How did Chimajiappa conquer the Portuguese territories?
answermarkup:
i. The Portuguese ruled over the territories of Vasai and Thane on the Konkan coast and oppressed their subjects.
ii. Chimajiappa, who was sent by Bajirao to conquer these territories conquered Thane and the adjacent areas.
iii. He laid siege to the Vasai fort, which was very strong and had powerful Portuguese artillery.
iv. Chimajiappa continued the siege with perseverance and forced the Portuguese to surrender the fort of Vasai and pass large parts of the Portuguese territory into the hands of the Marathas.

markup: How did the kingdoms of Vijaynagar and Bahamani emerge?
answermarkup: Kingdom of Vijaynagar: i) The brothers Harihar and Bukka, were Sardars in the service of Sultan Muhammad-bin-Tughluque during his reign in Delhi. ii) There occurred many revolts in the South against the Sultan. iii) In 1336 CE, taking advantage of the instability in the South, the two brothers - Harihar and Bukka, founded the kingdom of Vijaynagar in the South. iv) Harihar became the first king of the Vijaynagar Kingdom and Hampi in today's Karnataka was its capital. markup: What do you understand by Residuary Powers?
answermarkup:
i) Residuary Powers are special powers entrusted by the Constitution, to the Union Government.
ii) Our constitution has distributed the different subjects on which laws are to be made, between the Union Government and the State Governments.
iii) This distribution is done by dividing those various subjects into three lists as follows;
a. The Union List includes subject on which the Union Government makes laws
b. The State List which includes subjects on which the State Government makes laws, and
c. The Concurrent List which includes subjects on which both the State and Union Governments can make laws.
iv) If a subject comes up that is not included in any of these three lists, the Union Government is entitled to make laws on it. These powers of the Union Government are termed as Residuary Powers.

markup: How Shivaji Maharaj escaped from Panhalgad?

markup: Explain the emergence and fall of the Sultanate in North.

answermarkup:

markup: Provisions of the Constitution
answermarkup:
i) Constitution refers to a book that comprises of all the provisions regarding the administration of a country, mentioned together in a systematic way.
ii) The rules and provisions in the Constitution are the fundamental laws of the country.
iii) The provisions in the Constitution include a wide range of things viz. citizenship, the rights of citizens, the relationship between citizens and the State, subjects of the laws to be made by the governments, elections, restrictions on government, jurisdiction of the State, etc.
iv) While making laws, the government is bound to follow these provisions or else the Judiciary can declare those laws null and void or unconstitutional.
v) Each country creates such provisions which are not only suited to its needs and objectives, but also match its distinct nature.
vi) Governing a country with the help of rules or provisions has multiple benefits.
e.g.: It safeguards people's rights & freedoms and fixes their duties & responsibilities, prevents misuse of power, strengthens democracy and maintains peace.

markup: Raising the Maratha standard at Attock
answermarkup:
i. Najibkhan, a Rohilla chief, did not like the Maratha supremacy in the North.

markup: Escape from Agra
answermarkup:
i) To keep Shivaji Maharaj away from Deccan politics, Jaisingh proposed to Shivaji Maharaj that he should visit Agra and meet the Emperor.
ii) Shivaji Maharaj, accompanied by Prince Sambhaji and a few of his trusted people, set out for Agra.

markup: Siege of Jinji
answermarkup:
i. After the capture of Raigad, Aurangzeb sent Zulfikarkhan on the campaign of Jinji.
ii. He laid a siege but the Marathas bravely defended the fort for almost eight years.
iii. Santaji and Dhanaji of the Marathas fiercely attacked the Mughal forces engaged in the siege from outside.
iv. Though Rajaram Maharaj escaped through the siege and returned to Maharashtra but the fort of Jinji was captured by Zulfikarkhan.
4. The strategy implemented by Maharani Tarabai to capture Mughal Forts
Ans: i. Aurangzeb used his large army and captured many Maratha forts.
ii. The Marathas were comparatively weaker to combat Aurangzeb's huge army and to recapture the forts.
iii. Hence, Maharani Tarabai used an effective strategy against the Mughals. As per this strategy - As the rainy season would approach, the Killedar of the fort used to pretend to side with Aurangzeb, accept a bribe from him and hand over the fort to him. This bribe amount was then deposited in the Maratha treasury.
iv. Once Aurangzeb repleted the wealth, grains and ammunition on the fort, Tarabai used to attack and capture that fort.
This strategy of Tarabai is described as 'Safe deposit locker system'.

markup: The Directive Principles of State Policy
answermarkup:
i. The directive instructions to the State on how to achieve the goals expressed in the Preamble, through State policies are called as Directive Principles of State Policy.
ii. Through the Directive Principles of State Policy, the Constitution has specified the subjects to which the Union and State Governments should give priority in their policies for people's welfare.
iii. The makers of the Indian Constitution did not make the directives binding upon the State like the fundamental rights and expected that States should implement them slowly and steadily as implementing all these policies at the same time would require a lot of resources.

markup: Shivaji Maharaj's preparation for the Coronation
answermarkup:

markup: Shivaji Maharaj’s Care for the Ryot (People)

markup: The Bhosales of Nagpur
answermarkup:
i. During the reign of Shahu Maharaj, Parasoji Bhosale was given the jagir of Varhad and Gondawan.

markup: Sadashivraobhau
answermarkup:
i. Sadashivraobhau was the son of Chimajiappa and the cousin of Peshwa Nanasaheb.
ii. He had explained the broad viewpoint of the Marathas in his correspondence with the rulers in the North, that they were all native to the land. He had also stated that Abdali was an enemy from a foreign country. However, the northern rulers did not respond favourably to him and took a neutral stand.
iii. Later, Peshwa Nanasaheb sent Sadashivraobhau along with his eldest son Vishwasrao to the north to crush Abdali.

markup: Fraternity
answermarkup:
i) Fraternity means having a 'we-feeling' towards one another. It makes people become more understanding towards each others' problems and needs.
ii) Fraternity is closely related to human dignity and grows automatically in an atmosphere of mutual respect among the citizens.
iii) The makers of the Constitution believed that irrespective of the number of laws made in order to achieve the constitutional goals, fraternity is essential in realising these goals. Hence, fraternity was included as a goal in the Preamble.
iv) Fraternity will facilitate the task of bringing about a new society based on the values of justice and equality.

markup: The types of Justice as guaranteed by the Constitution.
answermarkup: i) Justice means abolishing injustice and ensuring that everybody has the opportunity to progress in the society. ii) Justice can only be achieved by adopting policies that will promote public good. iii) The three types of justice mentioned in the Preamble are as follows: a. Social Justice Social Justice implies all human beings have the right to the same dignity, status and respect. It states that there should be no discrimination among the citizens on the basis of caste, creed, race, language, region, place of birth or sex. b. Economic Justice Economic justice ensures everyone has the right to a source of livelihood, without any discrimination. For the eradication of poverty, our Constitution has given this right to every citizen. c. Political Justice Political justice means adopting Universal adult franchise wherein all citizens completing 18 years of age have the right to vote in elections. This principle enables equal participation by all the adults in the running of the country.

markup: Liberty
answermarkup:
i) Liberty is one of the values adopted by the Indian Constitution.
ii) Liberty means absence of coercive and unfair restrictions upon an individual and presence of an atmosphere conducive to the development of his/her inherent capacities.
iii) Freedom of thought and expression is an individual's most fundamental freedom. Everyone is free to express their own views and opinions.
iv) The liberty of belief, faith and worship is called as religious freedom. This gives us the freedom of celebrating the festivals and the freedom of faith and worship.
v) A democracy becomes mature only when citizens enjoy freedom.

markup: Parliamentary System of Government
answermarkup:

markup: Right to Equality
answermarkup:
i. The Right to Equality prohibits the State from discriminating among citizens on the basis of social status, gender, etc. It aims to establish equality in Indian society and applies equally to all.
ii. The State cannot discriminate while extending protections given by different laws.
E.g.: Protection from arrest without warrant.
iii. Also, for employment purposes such as government employment, there cannot be any discrimination on the grounds of religion, caste, race, sex, descent or place of birth or residence.
iv. Under the Right to Equality, the inhuman practice of untouchability has been abolished by law and is a cognizable offence.
v. Titles like Raja, Maharaja, Raobahadur, etc. that create an artificial hierarchy among people have also been abolished.

markup: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
answermarkup:
i) Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are two sides of the same coin.
ii) Rights give citizens freedom, while Directives guide the State to provide welfare.
iii) Both together help in achieving justice, liberty, and equality in society.
iv) They ensure that democracy in India is strong, active, and people-oriented.

markup: Chandbibi

markup: Shivaji Maharaj - a ruler concerned about the welfare of his subjects

markup: Chronicles
answermarkup:
i) Chronicles are a written documentation of the events that had happened in the past. They are a type of written source of history.
ii) Chronicles are sometimes written many years after the event had occurred and are hence seen to rely on hearsays.
iii) Chronicles help us to understand various aspects like contemporary political happenings, linguistic transactions, cultural life and social conditions of a particular place during a particular period.
iv) Bakhar is one such type of chronicle that originated in Maharashtra. Other examples of such chronicles are Mahikavatichi Bakhar, Sabhasad Bakhar, Chitnisachi Bakhar, Bhausahebachi Bakhar, etc.
v) The work of some contemporary western historians like Robert Arm, M. C. Sprengel and Grant Duff is also noteworthy.

markup: The work done by Ahilyabai Holkar
answermarkup:

answermarkup:

markup: The Directive Principles of the Constitution enumerated in the textbook.
answermarkup:
i. The directive instructions specified by the Constitution to the State on how to achieve the goals, expressed in the Preamble, are called as Directive Principles of State Policy.
ii. The Directive Principles of the Constitution enumerated in the textbook are as follows:
a. The State must ensure sufficient means of livelihood for all citizens without any gender discrimination.
b. The State must ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
c. The State must ensure that the public health improves.
d. The State must ensure the protection and improvement of the environment by safeguarding the forests and wild-life of the country.
e. The State should protect all monuments of historic interest and national importance.
f. The State should promote, with special care, the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the society, especially the Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
g. The State should offer public assistance to citizens in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, etc.
h. The State should secure a uniform civil code applicable to the entire country.

markup: Shivaji Maharaj's policy regarding agriculture
answermarkup:
: i) Shivaji Maharaj knew the importance of agriculture, which was the main occupation of the people in villages. So he paid attention to the welfare of the farmers and encouraged peasants to bring more land under cultivation.
ii) He entrusted the responsibility of organizing the land revenue system to his experienced officer Annaji Datto and warned his officers that they should not collect more revenue than that was fixed.
iii) Remissions were granted by him in land revenue and other taxes, if the crop was lost due to excessive rains or drought, or invasion by an enemy army.
iv) Maharaj had also instructed his officers to provide peasants with bullocks, ploughs and good seeds for sowing.
Thus, Shivaji Maharaj ensured the development of agriculture.

markup: Material Sources
answermarkup:
i) Material sources comprise of different objects, different places and their ruins. These sources provide insights about the period to which they belonged.
ii) A style of the building construction memorials, forts, copper plates, coins, inscriptions, cave, sculptures, and monuments, tell us about the development of architecture and people's standard of living in that particular period. Objects like weapons, utensils, ornaments, clothes, decorative articles, toys, implements, musical instruments tell us about the day-to-day lives of the people in that period. Places like chaityas, viharas, temples, churches, mosques, agiaries, durgahs, mukbaras and gurudwaras tell us about the religious beliefs of the people in that period.
iii) Coins tell us a lot about the rulers, their period, governance, religious ideas, their personal details, the financial transactions at that time, metallurgy, the religious co-ordination and the use of language in that period.
iv) An inscription is an important and reliable source of history as it tells us about the language, script and social life of a particular period.

markup: Painting during the Peshwa period
answermarkup:

iii. The famous temples located at Pandeshwar, Morgaon, Pal, Benwadi, Pashan near Pune have paintings on the walls. The themes of the mentioned paintings were Dashavatara, Ganapati, Shankar, Rampanchayatana, mythological stories, Ramayana, Mahabharata, festivals and so on.
iv. Jin Charitra paintings adorned the Jain temple, at Jamod in Vidarbha. Illustrations in the pothis, minatures, portraits, scenes, etc. were also painted.

markup: Dattaji Shinde

markup: The after effects of the battle of Panipat
answermarkup:
i. On 14 January 1761, the Marathas opened the third battle of Panipat, by attacking Abdali's army.

Marathas overcame this great defeat of Panipat and revived their supremacy in the politics of the North.

markup: Balaji Vishwanath

markup: Right against Exploitation
answermarkup:
i. Generally women, children, the weaker sections of society and powerless people are exploited. The Right against Exploitation equally enables everyone to stand up against any kind of exploitation.
ii. Exploitation includes bonded labour or forcing somebody to work against his/ her wish, treating somebody like a slave, denying them legitimate compensation, making them do excessive or strenuous work, starving them or ill-treating them.
iii. It bans all types of oppression and exploitation.
iv. There is a special provision to specifically prevent the exploitation of children. Accordingly, children under the age of 14 years cannot be employed in hazardous places like factories and mines.

markup: Directive Principles of State Policy
answermarkup:

markup: Shahu Maharaj
answermarkup:
i. The Mughals had kept Shahu Maharaj captive after they captured Raigad in 1689. He was under Prince Azamshah's captive after the death of Emperor Aurangzeb.

iii. When Tarabai did not accept Shahu Maharaj's claim to the throne, the armies of Shahu Maharaj and Maharani Tarabai fought a battle at Khed on the bank of the Bheema river. Shahu Maharaj won the battle, crowned himself and made Satara the capital of the Maratha kingdom.
iv. He knew the politics, strengths and weaknesses of the North and the Mughals well, as he had spent the early part of his life in the Mughal camps. He was acquainted with many influential people in the Mughal court.
v. Along with Peshwa Balaji and Peshwa Bajirao, he expanded the Maratha kingdom and its power in the North. He gave a new direction to the Maratha politics in the changing circumstances.

markup: Sant Dnyaneshwar
answermarkup:
a) He was a great Sant of the Varkari movement. He gave the Varkari movement the prestige of a religion.
